name: HUMAN Security (PerimeterX) hidden iframe
plain: A hidden iframe from li.protechts.net runs HUMAN's bot detection with a hash of LinkedIn's browser ID.
meaning: A third-party vendor runs its own behavior and device checks in the page and sets its own cookies, tied to the person through a hash of LinkedIn's bcookie.

access.persistence: Cookies _pxvid, _pxmvid, _pxhd, _pxde, pxcts, _px<id>, _pxff_<id>, _pxttld per LinkedIn cookie table
steps: LIX flag pemberly.tracking.human.integration loads the iframe (id humanThirdPartyIframe)
HUMAN script collects its own device and behavior signals
Cookies set under LinkedIn's domain for risk scoring
d_id is SHA256 of bcookie so HUMAN can join its data to LinkedIn's browser ID

limits.headline: Can run a hidden bot check on LinkedIn pages and tie it to its browser ID
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a LinkedIn page loads
can: Load a hidden frame from a security company during the page visit
Score whether you look like a person or a bot
Send a scrambled version of LinkedIn's browser ID with the check
cannot: Show you anything, since the frame is hidden
See your files, other tabs or other apps
Run if the page or its frames are blocked, though blocking may break the page
Name you on its own without the LinkedIn ID

story.what_it_is: A hidden frame from a security firm runs bot checks on the page and sets its own cookies.
story.for_you: You never see this hidden frame. It runs checks on how your device and mouse behave, and sets its own cookie. The security firm links its data to you through a code made from LinkedIn's browser ID.
story.for_makers: Bots cost LinkedIn real money and trust, so it hires a specialist to spot them. The vendor learns patterns across many sites, and that sharpens the score. A critic notes the vendor also gets a link to a person.

use_cases.example: A script posing as a person tries to log in thousands of times, and the bot checks give each try a risk score.
A bot solves LinkedIn Games puzzles at superhuman speed to climb a leaderboard, and the checks help catch it.
A bot clicks a paid ad over and over, and the checks mark those clicks invalid so the advertiser is not billed.
A fake account sends spam invites, and the checks notice the browser does not behave like a human one.
Ticket and sneaker sites use the same kind of check to block bots that buy stock before people can.
A team removes bot traffic from its reports so real person numbers are accurate.

risks: Third party sees device and behavior data
Tied to your LinkedIn ID by a hash

technical_bounds: Exact HUMAN signal set is not published
BleepingComputer could not verify further sharing beyond the iframe

abuse: Third party gets a browser keyed identifier

linkedin.how: Verified in the snapshot (iframe URL, app ids, id humanThirdPartyIframe). LinkedIn's cookie table lists the _px cookies. What HUMAN collects inside is not documented publicly.
